987.t: Writing the horn chart on Springsteen's 'Tenth Avenue Freeze-Out'
987.s: Blank paper on the stands; Steve Van Zandt's ideas were transcribed into the chart.
987.q: Well yeah, we had to do some writing sometimes, and on some very good records. This one always comes to mind, on “Born to Run” the Bruce Springsteen record. It was me, Mike and Sanborn and a great trombone player, Wayne Andre. We showed up at the session and there was music paper on our stands but…

987.s: James Taylor wrote horn parts on graph paper and the horn men transcribed them.
987.q: You just never knew what kind of situation — I had another good one in mind, I’m trying to think of it now. Oh for instance — and these all ended up great records. James Taylor — we were close with him at one point, especially Barry was a close friend. And we did now I don’t know if I’ll remember…

441.t: Playing on Herb Alpert, Sinatra and other pop records
441.s: Jolly recalls double-piano with Burt Bacharach on This Guy's in Love with You and other hit dates.
441.q: Well there were two pianos. It was Burt and I playing. It was Burt Bacarach and I, yeah. I don’t remember — I think we were both doing the same thing.

441.t: The Frank Zappa date and Ian Underwood
441.s: He recounts a late-night session for Zappa's Lumpy Gravy, Zappa's praise, and Ian Underwood's synthesizer mastery.
441.q: I’m trying to think of these names that I’ve worked with, it’s a lot of years. And you know what he said to me when I was on the date? It was a late date, it didn’t start until like one o’clock or eleven thirty at night. And I remember leaving the house and thinking oh boy, it’s going to be one of…

996.t: Producer Michael Lloyd, Belinda Carlisle and Dirty Dancing
996.s: He worked with producer Michael Lloyd, played on 'Mad About You' and on the Dirty Dancing album.
996.q: Well in L.A. I did a lot of work, and still do, with a producer named Michael Lloyd who’s very, very pop. He’s a very pop producer. He did like teen stars in the 70s — Shaun Cassidy and Leif Garrett and people like that. But we did a lot of stuff, especially in the 80s. Belinda Carlisle’s first…

996.t: Muppets, Clooney, Alan Parsons sessions; the call from McCartney
996.s: He lists artists he played with, tells of the Great Gonzo session, the Clooney record, an Abbey Road session, and the call to audition for McCartney.
996.q: Yeah. And that was all in the space of a couple of years then, you know, back in the 70s. I mean it goes way beyond that. I mean three out of the four Beatles. I played with at least two Muppets, actually more than two Muppets. I played banjo for some of Kermit’s stuff —

822.t: Peter Tosh session on Saturday Night Live
822.s: Rowe tests Marini's memory of recorded credits; Marini discovers in a reggae bar that he played the solo on Peter Tosh's 'Wanted Dread or Alive'.
822.q: Yeah you know what’s funny about that is my wife and I were on vacation in St. John’s and we were going into Cruise Bay and we discovered this Surf Bar that played nothing but reggae and it was really a cool bar. And we were in there one night. We’d been in there a couple of times before, and this…

822.t: Meat Loaf session and a written solo
822.s: Marini recalls a Meat Loaf session where the producer had written out the solo.
822.q: Yeah. You know I remember that too. It’s funny that you picked that one because Meat Loaf, that music, it’s like Bruce Springsteen to me. Clarence Clemmons could play a great solo at the drop of a hat. That stuff for me, I have so much difficulty trying to play a solo over that kind of stuff. And I…

1004.t: Spotting hits: Burt Bacharach and Dion at Bell Sound
1004.s: Bacharach and Hal David asked her which side was a hit; both sides of a Dion record took off.
1004.q: Yeah. Some Burt Bacharach things. Because I did a lot for Burt. And I remember being at Bell Sound, there was a guy named Domenick Romeo who did all of the mastering right there. They did the mastering there. And I was walking past his room and Burt and Hal were there and they said, “Annie come in…

1004.t: Doing good work on songs she did not love; Little Eva
1004.s: She rarely recalls disliked demos; Little Eva's Locomotion demo became the hit master.
1004.q: No. But I can hardly remember pieces that I didn’t like. There was one demo I did which was a sort of an oddball thing from some other studio. And I think it was Liberace’s brother had a company that said, “We’ll set your song to music.” So people would send in lyrics and they would put them to the…

215.t: Acoustic guitar overdub on 'The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face'
215.s: Bucky recognizes an overdub he played to accompany an already-recorded vocal, without knowing it would be a hit.
215.ch: Session stories and why he was hired
215.q: Yeah. Well they asked me to do something without the music, and that’s what I did.

215.t: Publishing-house songwriters and recording "Stand By Me"
215.s: Nevins' publishing house churned out songs for Connie Francis; Pizzarelli did three sessions a day and forgot playing on "Stand By Me".
215.ch: New York studio and TV work
215.q: And all Al would do is pick up the phone and call Connie Francis or somebody, “Hey we need a tenth song for the album.” Boom they shoot down and they had demos made. They made them down in the cellar of the same building, churn them out. Neil Sedaka was one of the writers too. They all became very,…

408.s: A twenty-minute session in L.A. followed by a fog-delayed flight home.
408.ch: Pop sessions and the hit-record question
408.q: somewhere with a quintet … [Phil’s cat makes scratching noises as she plays nearby] Oh my god [chuckles] what’s she doing? … Hey, get down!

408.s: Phil Ramone asks for one minute of fast bebop in B flat.
408.ch: Pop sessions and the hit-record question
408.q: Around the same period, yeah, when uh Phil Ramone called me and said, “I need you to play one minute of bebop, fast.” I said “What key?” He said, “B flat,” I said, “Okay.” [both laugh] If it’s a rock ‘n’ roll thing it could have been in B, and he said, “I need some ’I Got Rhythm,’ fast,” I said “B…

885.t: Sessions with Allen Toussaint, including Working in the Coal Mine
885.s: He drummed on the original Working in the Coal Mine, and the interviewer asks about overdubs and a Coca-Cola commercial.
885.q: I was on the original, working on the drums. Alan went to New York with the record, and they thought it was three drummers was on that, and it was the only one. Some very intricate things that he had going on at the time. I was young and flexible, but it came out.

510.t: Playing Syndrum for six hours on a Mick Jagger record
510.s: Having brought every percussion instrument, Alias is asked only to play Syndrum fills for six hours on a Jagger solo track.
510.ch: Jaco, Weather Report and pop work
510.q: Oh I wish I could have done that. But Mick Jagger was really a funny scene. That was another funny scene. There was a producer there, Armenian or some kind of name that ended in I-A-N — something Franconian or I don’t know, the only reason why I say that is because he was ethnically Far Eastern or…

201.t: Playing on Ricky Martin's She Bangs
201.s: A studio story about the title and the hit record.
201.q: I remember in the studio, I’m in the studio and I’ve got this music in front of me it says “She Bangs,” and like I’m the oldest guy in the horn section of the thing and I says, “Jesus, when I was a kid,” I said, “I never heard that expression.” I says, “The expression I heard when I was a kid was…

674.t: Recording tuba and whistles for Springsteen's Seeger Sessions
674.s: He describes being called to overdub tuba and whistles at Springsteen's studio and a follow-up session.
674.q: You know and sometimes it’s fun and sometimes like where’s the beat. Plus playing tuba, it’s like a bass thing. So if it’s not in there, and I really had to hear what the bass player was doing. It was so easy. I’m in a recording studio, they sent a limo to my house in New York to go to South Jersey…

314.t: Session lengths and hearing himself on 'American Pie'
314.s: Dates ran three hours with overtime; he recalls playing on 'American Pie' with Paul Griffin.
314.q: Recording dates were three hours, usually with a possible overtime. But sometimes they went on and on, which was good because I could pay the tuition.

495.s: He recalls how Bacharach appreciated his classical guitar fills.
495.q: Well I guess Burt Bachrach. I would consider him pop music. I mean it was good music in its own way. And he used to really get carried away with whatever little thing I did. “Oh man, you hear what he did there — bing!” Or something like that. And I loved it. And of course it was nice to be…

973.t: Lightnin' Strikes with Lou Christie and The Angels
973.s: Prompted by Lou Christie's obituary, he describes working out the record at the piano with The Angels and having Artie Schroeck orchestrate.
973.q: Well we actually made that record at the piano. The group that we used were The Angels – Peggy Farina, they had the hit record, “My Boyfriend’s Back,” but we used them as background singers. And they sang on all the records I did with Lou Christie. And we would get together, because they didn’t…

496.t: Rod Stewart and Gladys Knight sessions with stand-in vocalists
496.s: Finck says singers like Stewart and Knight often did not attend, with Vaneese Thomas tracking vocals as a reference.
496.q: He was on one or two sessions that we did in Los Angeles. For the most part no. Someone else tracked his vocals for him.

559.s: He was on the Kodachrome album and recalls Steve Gadd, Richard Davis, Hubert Laws, Jerome Richardson and others.
559.q: It didn’t happen in the car but I’ll tell you what the tunes that I was on were on the “Kodachrome” album. So I was at — this community that I live in they had a guy come in the other night and sing tunes and play guitar. And I turned to the woman next to me and I said, “I was on that album.” So…

719.t: Nik Kershaw and the horns on Wouldn't It Be Good
719.s: Hey admires Nik Kershaw and explains how horns came to be added to his record, playing to the guitar solo.
719.q: Oh my God. Nik Kershaw to me was the hope for music, pop music, back in the day. Great tunes, great changes, wonderful melodies, interesting ideas. He was — it was incredible. We went to hear him live a couple of times and it was just like wow, I hope this is where music goes. And then he decided…

212.s: His story of Lennon's horn section stalling until he suggested the arrangement, then arranging the rest; Lennon's secrecy and fans.
212.q: Oh I’d say everything. It was a horn section. John had the track all ready and we were going to put horns on it. And he had this idea that he explained to us that horn players are real musicians, not like guys who just play guitar and drums and that sort of thing. And if you put a bunch of them…

696.t: Memorable sessions: Patti LaBelle, Paul McCartney, the Meters
696.s: Late-1960s to 80s sessions with saxophonist Alvin Thomas and trumpeter John Longo, including Patti LaBelle, McCartney's Venus and Mars, Neville Brothers and Meters; he played on Lady Marmalade.
696.q: Oh quite a few of them man. The one that I did like from the late sixties up to the end of the seventies, even into the eighties. I had a friend of mine who was a saxophone player, he died in ’78 of lymphatic cancer. And we did a lot of sessions together in New Orleans. There was another trumpet…

889.s: He plays the famous three notes; the brass was overdubbed after the rhythm section, not knowing it was a million-seller.
889.q: Three famous notes, I’ve done so many things in my career. Now my students call me up after that — he heard that — he said, “Oh Mr. Porrello, you’re awesome” for those three notes.

523.s: Raph describes playing on many rock and roll dates without knowing whose they were, including Blood, Sweat & Tears and Bob Dylan.
523.q: I did stuff for Blood, Sweat & Tears, I did stuff for Bob Dylan. Who’s the guy with the raindrops? Not Burt Bacharach, the other guy.

661.t: Lip syncing with Cyndi Lauper and New Paradise
661.s: She was the fake drummer in Cyndi Lauper's promotional videos and sang for lip-syncing French singers in New Paradise.
661.q: Yeah. Mainly I worked with Cyndi Lauper, I worked in her band for four years in the 90s. And we would do a lot of promotional stuff. So when we did the promotional stuff it was, she’d have all females and I was the drummer. I was the fake drummer. So, and they’d put a little mic there you know, so…

488.t: Playing on Van Morrison's Astral Weeks
488.s: Recalls the shy Van Morrison, the players (Connie Kay, Richard Davis), lead sheets and the few days of sessions.
488.ch: Teaching, studio work and race in New York
488.q: I remember a little guy came from Ireland and did something called “Astral Weeks.” What was this guy’s name? Tell me his name.

597.t: Lucretia MacEvil solo constructed by Bobby Colomby
597.s: The solo was heavily punched in and constructed by producer Bobby Colomby.
597.q: That solo was actually — God that solo, there were so many touches in that solo. Bobby Colomby produced that tune, and he would punch in here and punch in there, and that solo was very, very constructed by Bobby. I mean I like the way it came out, but it was very constructed by Bobby and I always…

469.t: The Copacabana recording with Barry Manilow
469.s: Recording Manilow's Copacabana in New York and L.A. with Paul Shaffer and Will Lee.
469.q: You know something? I wasn’t even sure we were recording that night you know. It was weird man because there was always gear around, people’s gear and mics and things you know, it was always around, lights. And I just played the show. It was like oh we’re just playing the show. You know.

376.t: Paul Simon and Phil Ramone's Night Game session
376.s: He tells how Phil Ramone got him on Simon's album and about his worry that he had laid an egg.
376.q: Well, that was… Paul Simon and the producer, Phil Ramone. Outstanding. I don’t know if he… but he’s the one of those Sinatra things with Bono. [laughs] Those duets, I mean. I mean, big time, you know. And he was also the producer, music producer for Paul Simon. And he said, told Paul Simon… I was…
